warnings.warning: The Summary says depth, salinity, oxygen, and pH are considered, but only temperature is used downstream and their units or role never enter a fitted interface.
The filter removes only -99.99 sentinels; it does not implement the prose claim that physically invalid values were screened.
The regional bounds include land and multiple national regimes, but no land-ocean mask or sampling-support map is retained.
The example record is at 299 m while the species discussion emphasizes shallower operating depths; depth selection is not shown in the printed filter.
NOAA is named only at organization level, so product version, query, stations, measurement methods, and immutable source identity remain missing.
Yearly averaging discards the monthly and seasonal timing needed to distinguish fishing seasons and temperature-driven movement.
The text describes 40 years from 1980 to 2019 but also prints 'from 1980 ... to 2019 to 2019'; the year-to-sheet mapping is not audited.
Appendix 1 groups coordinates after rounding to two decimals and exact equality, but does not quantify spatial aggregation error or duplicate station effects.
The country workbook and 37 data workbooks required by Appendix 1 are absent, so its annual means cannot be reproduced.
Appendix 2 uses background(i*k,j) rather than a documented year-block row index when reconstructing histories, creating a likely indexing error.
Appendix 2 assigns random values to data4(:,1) twice, overwriting observed latitude and making every run spatially different.
The second random coordinate assignment covers 51-71 and the random longitude covers -44-10, so retained histories are detached from their measured locations.
Zero is used as a missing-data marker even though zero degrees C is physically possible in the study region.
The paper states 54 representative positions but provides neither their observed coordinates nor the exact completeness calculation that selected them.
The Appendix 3 year vector omits 2012 and ends in 2017, conflicting with the claimed 1980-2019 history.
The code contains t=zeros(length(end)) and y=zeros(length(end)), which is not a valid declaration of arrays sized to the selected observations.
Fitting absolute calendar year squared yields very large correlated terms; no centering, scaling, condition number, or coefficient stability check is reported.
The fixed sin(year)+cos(year) term has no selected period and does not represent an annual seasonal cycle after the data were aggregated by year.
All 54 locations use the same functional family without residual plots, holdout years, parameter tables, or forecast intervals.
The paper extrapolates roughly fifty years beyond the fitting record without climate forcing, trend constraint, or long-horizon validation.
The paper says four interpolation methods were compared but supplies no error metric, withheld points, boundary test, or reason for choosing griddata v4.
Appendix 4 adds an external canshu1.xlsx vector to predictions, but the file, meaning, and derivation are not disclosed.
The interpolation grid includes land and extrapolates outside the convex support without a coastline mask or uncertainty.
Figures 5-7 use visually similar panels but do not expose common z-axis or color limits clearly enough to support temporal comparison.
Temperature-contour points are selected by observation and called rough, so the route regression begins from an undocumented subjective sample.
The polynomial order k, coefficients, selected coordinates, residuals, and goodness-of-fit are absent.
The paper does not state whether longitude predicts latitude or vice versa, even though one species route may not be single-valued under that orientation.
Stationary first derivatives identify candidate extrema but do not by themselves guarantee a unique least-squares solution or numerical stability.
Appendix 8 is cited for route fitting, but the shown code fits Norway and Iceland boundary curves rather than the two fish migration curves in Figure 8.
Temperature-qualified cells are treated as likely fish locations without population observations, abundance, occupancy probabilities, currents, food, spawning, or dispersal.
The assumed mackerel 8-16 degrees C and herring 12-18 degrees C bands overlap substantially, yet the manual route selection does not explain species separation.
Figure 10 contains a mackerel title but its caption says Moving Path of Herring, weakening species traceability.
Table 3 provides decadal representative points but the later annual crisis and legal calculations do not disclose interpolation between those points.
The paper discusses species depth ranges but uses surface-style maps with no three-dimensional habitat or vertical-temperature interface.
The model name changes among Macleaf, Mark Reeve, and Mark leaf, leaving the intended method identity unclear.
The body bins rates at 0.03 while Appendix 5 multiplies relative change by 1000 and uses 0.3, so thresholds and units are inconsistent.
The rapid-decline prose and code inequalities do not consistently include equality at the negative threshold.
Appendix 5 adds an undocumented random 10-20 degree baseline to every location before computing transition states.
No random seed is fixed, so the state history and any claimed probability can change between runs.
The fifth departure-state total repeats the condition for the second group, so rapid-decline transitions are not accumulated as intended.
The e array is initialized as 5 by number-of-locations while inner logic indexes transition columns, producing an unclear and potentially invalid layout.
When a row count is zero the code writes to e(5,...) regardless of the origin state, mixing probability rows.
Zero entries are filled from external canshu.xlsx rather than estimated with a declared smoothing prior.
No actual one-step matrix is printed for any location, so the 2032 and 2050 probabilities cannot be traced.
Appendix 5 repeatedly applies h=h.*e elementwise, not pi_n=pi_0 E^n matrix propagation.
The propagated variable h is never connected to an annual temperature, suitable cell, route coordinate, or stopping year.
The loop applies six multiplications without explaining how six steps produce a 2020-2070 annual forecast.
The final endd vector flattens entries of e, so its maximum and minimum are transition entries rather than exit-event probabilities.
The 666.72 km quantity uses all 36 hours as one-way travel, although a catch must be reached, handled, and returned while fresh.
Weather, currents, fishing time, loading, port approach, vessel downtime, and speed variability are ignored.
Model preparation says refrigerated vessels preserve fish for 3-4 days, while Section 6.2 changes this to 4-5 days.
A single radius is applied to herring and mackerel despite the assumption that their spoilage and handling may differ in practice.
The event scan uses a union range of 8-18 degrees C rather than separate species bands, so one species can mask the other's loss.
The paper never prints the annual temperature update, location probabilities, number of simulations, or event denominator.
From 2020 to 2032 is 12 years and to 2050 is 30 years, not the reported 13 and 31 years.
The reported 30 percent and 21.91 percent do not arise from any shown distribution, matrix, or geographic simulation.
Appendix 5 prints max(endd)-0.7 and min(endd)+0.2, arbitrary offsets that do not establish 30 percent or 21.91 percent.
The displayed spherical formula mixes x2 longitude with y2 latitude and uses x1-y1 instead of a longitude difference.
The displayed expression returns an angle but omits multiplication by Earth radius while the tables report kilometers.
The external SphereDist function used for reported distances is not included in the appendices.
Solution A selects a port with Euclidean distance in longitude-latitude degrees, then evaluates it with an undisclosed spherical routine.
Table 7 and Figure 15 select Orkney, but Section 6.3 Option A recommends Lerwick.
The one-port objective sums all 12 species-decade points equally without probability, catch value, season, fleet capacity, or route uncertainty.
Calling the result financially economical is unsupported because no relocation, port, fuel, labor, vessel, or revenue terms enter the objective.
Solution B optimizes each decade independently and therefore ignores the cost and feasibility of moving among Orkney, Stornoway, Scrabster, and Lerwick.
Table 10 repeats the Orkney 2020 coordinate but lists 850.39 km for herring, conflicting with Table 9's 167.53 km from the same port-year.
Table 10's 2020 and later distances appear shifted or misaligned across fish and years, so the upgrade calendar is not reproducible.
The decadal port model assigns equal species importance and does not include quotas, expected catch, prices, port capacity, or national boundaries.
The paper introduces 4-5 refrigerated days but never computes or compares the implied 1777.92-2222.4 km travel range.
The upgrade indicator compares with the old range only; it does not demonstrate that any proposed new vessel can complete the route.
The Summary says new vessels are needed in 2020 for Option A, while the Orkney distance table first exceeds the old range for herring in 2050.
The recommendation has no fleet size, purchase cost, financing, refrigeration temperature, energy, capacity, maintenance, or emissions model.
The printed Mahalanobis expression ends with mu-mu and is therefore identically zero for every fish location.
Even the standard Mahalanobis distance to a boundary-point cloud is not an inside-polygon or territorial-sea test.
The prose says a smaller distance means entry, while Appendix 8 selects distances greater than 6350 and 2530.
Appendix 8 scales the fraction of dense curve sample points above a threshold by 91, rather than testing 91 annual fish positions.
The thresholds 6350 and 2530 are unexplained and depend on boundary sampling density, coordinate ordering, and covariance.
Figure 1 and Reference 2 concern EEZs, while the prose repeatedly claims territorial seas; these are different legal zones.
Table 11 labels its output no fishing time but derives fish-route geometry, not actual company fishing activity or access permission.
The negotiation recommendation has no quota, treaty, licensing, enforcement, cost, or revenue-impact model.
Figure 18 is called the true migration path but only supports qualitative directions; no coordinate pairs, dates, errors, or independent holdout are compared.
The claim that qualitative visual consistency makes the model correct and effective exceeds the validation performed.
The BP network has no architecture, training labels, split, objective, threshold, repetitions, or performance metric.
A twenty-year BP output merely lies inside a wide 2032-2050 interval and is not independent evidence for either endpoint probability.
The AHP scoring model is proposed conditionally but no pairwise matrix, weights, consistency ratio, option scores, or result is reported.
The back and cross misjudgment rates lack sample size, classes, confusion matrices, folds, uncertainty, and a link to the 29/11-year outputs.
Despite the section title, no input is varied and no sensitivity curve, elasticity, uncertainty interval, or decision reversal is shown.
The limitations section names only vessel-speed heterogeneity and omits dominant data, forecast, route, probability, economic, and legal uncertainties.
The magazine says Scotland may have no fish to catch as soon as 13 years, carrying the off-by-one clock and scenario claim into public communication.
The article says herring will migrate to Shetland within this year, but the body route table does not establish that event or its uncertainty.
The public Solution A map and prose use one new location, but do not disclose the body's Lerwick-Orkney contradiction or economic omissions.
The magazine recommends new fishing vessels without cost, capability, or fleet evidence and relies on a generic vessel photograph.
Only three references are listed for data, biology, maritime geometry, validation imagery, law, ports, vessel performance, and public claims.
A source placeholder appears as 's ### URL' in the territorial-water section, leaving the boundary provenance unresolved.
The appendices publish code fragments but not the data workbooks, canshu files, fitted parameters, software version, or executable environment.
Random coordinates and temperatures make the published code nondeterministic and sever source-to-result provenance.
Several Appendix 5 branches use inconsistent indices and overwritten arrays, so equation-code parity is not demonstrated.
The final map code plots broad corner points and sampled curves but does not implement official 12-nautical-mile territorial polygons.

global_organization_chain: Summary compresses warming stakes -> NOAA preprocessing -> field forecast -> species routes -> state probabilities -> exit years -> relocation/vessel options -> foreign-water negotiation.
Introduction establishes global and local stakes, then restates all five official requirements before any technical choice.
Model preparation fixes map scope, species thermal bands, port candidates, vessel endurance, assumptions, and notation as the typed input contract.
Problem 1 moves from screened annual location histories through location-wise extrapolation and spatial interpolation to contour-selected least-squares routes and decadal coordinates.
Problem 2 turns annual temperature rates into five states, transition probabilities, a Scrabster operating circle, and two claimed range-exit cases.
Problem 3 compares one-port and decadal relocation tables, then uses port-to-species distance tables to motivate refrigerated vessels and a phased business calendar.
Problem 4 converts fitted routes and sampled Iceland/Norway boundaries into Mahalanobis-style classifications, year counts, and a negotiation recommendation.
Evaluation introduces qualitative route comparison, BP, AHP, and classifier errors; limitations and promotion follow before the two-page public article.
Appendices 1-8 expose the implementation boundary, including data workbooks, random replacements, fit function, state loops, port objectives, and boundary thresholds.

main_argument_chains.claim: Historical regional temperature records can be extrapolated and spatially interpolated to create future temperature-qualified routes for herring and mackerel.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Decadal route coordinates become the shared input for range, port, vessel, and foreign-water decisions, subject to data and population-model boundaries.
support_steps: Filter and annually aggregate NOAA-style records.
Retain sufficiently observed locations.
Fit and extrapolate each location through 2070.
Interpolate decadal fields.
Select species-qualified points and fit separate curves.

main_argument_chains.claim: Temperature-rate uncertainty and unrefrigerated endurance bound when the current company loses practical access.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: The paper reports 2032 and 2050 as worst and best cases, while the missing probability closure remains explicit.
support_steps: Discretize annual rates into five states.
Count one-step transitions.
Propagate future state probabilities.
Convert 1.5 days and 10 knots to 666.72 km.
Scan for no suitable location inside the circle.

main_argument_chains.claim: Relocation and refrigerated vessels can keep two species within operating reach.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: The company receives two operational structures, but costs, table consistency, and vessel capability remain unresolved.
support_steps: List 25 candidate ports.
Choose one port over all route points.
Choose a port per decade for paired species.
Compare distance tables with old-vessel range.
Assemble a phased calendar and processing alternative.

main_argument_chains.claim: Foreign-water exposure and public communication are required consequences of the forecast routes.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Legal access and public strategy enter the decision, with maritime-zone and classifier limitations retained.
support_steps: Sample Icelandic and Norwegian boundaries.
Fit boundary curves and calculate Mahalanobis distances.
Threshold the distances and scale counts to years.
Recommend negotiation.
Translate the chain into a two-page magazine article.

visualization_dispositions.analytical_purpose: Five dense paragraphs compress the NOAA-to-route, state-to-exit, port-and-vessel, and foreign-water chains with endpoint years and probabilities.
The contents expose a four-problem progression, separate evaluation sections, a two-page public deliverable, and thirteen appendix pages.
An EEZ overview highlights Scotland and neighboring states, establishing geography but not territorial-sea polygons.
Paired herring and mackerel drawings support the plain-language species-preference setup.
A labeled Scotland map places the candidate ports later used in the relocation tables.
Four boxes connect preprocessing, location-wise time fitting, shelf-point forecasting, and route extraction.
One NOAA-style row exposes coordinates, year, month, day, time, depth, temperature, salinity, oxygen, pH, and country.
A seven-line brace lists regional bounds and sentinel exclusions, making the stated preprocessing rule inspectable.
Four 3D panels show 1980, 1990, 2000, and 2010 fields without clearly stated common z limits.
Six 3D panels continue 2020-2070 and visually suggest changing surfaces.
Ten aligned contour panels provide the visual basis from which route points are manually selected.
Polynomial definition, discrete pairs, squared-error objective, and stationary conditions form a compact algebra chain.
Side-by-side coordinate plots show separate blue fitted paths and red selected points for herring and mackerel.
Species, year, latitude, longitude, and named sea area make the trajectory output typed and auditable.
A North Atlantic basemap labels herring decadal positions moving northwest toward Iceland.
A parallel map labels mackerel positions moving northeast, although the printed caption repeats herring.
The loop connects boat origin, range, state probabilities, suitability, and event output but leaves the simulation mechanism implicit.
A green circle centered near northern Scotland visualizes the claimed 666.72 km operating radius.
Two rows place 2032/30 percent and 2050/21.91 percent side by side without a displayed distribution.
Candidate ports branch into one-location and decadal relocation plans before a vessel-upgrade recommendation.
A 25-row coordinate table and labeled map expose the complete candidate set.
Radians conversions and an arccos expression make the distance interface visible for last-pass symbol checking.
One-port and six-decade port tables are paired with route-and-port maps for direct option comparison.
Species-specific distance columns compare each plan against the old-vessel threshold and reveal row inconsistencies.
A decision loop converts route points and a Mahalanobis criterion into inside/outside years.
The displayed classifier formula, two year counts, a curve plot, and a geographic map expose the full legal-result chain.
Two sourced route diagrams provide only a qualitative direction comparison for the paper's external-validation claim.
A two-column local-news layout combines fishermen imagery, species route maps, a crisis narrative, and a global-warming sidebar.
A vessel hero image, five-pound-note hook, Solution A/B maps, and option text form a public-facing recommendation page.
Thirteen syntax-highlighted pages reveal workbook dependencies, random replacements, fit functions, transition branches, port objectives, and territorial thresholds.
